pr_title: Improves history request speed in backtest mode for python algorithms.
pr_body:
#### Description
- Implements `QCAlgorithm.py`: serves as an interface between the python algorithms and the C# engine. The QCAlgorithm class implements a History method that overrides those from C# QCAlgorithm.
  - Updates python algorithms accordingly.
- Implements `PandasHistoryRequest` class. This class is used to gather the necessary information to manage the pandas data frame that is created by reading local files.
- Implements new methods in `QCAlgorithm.cs`: `CreateHistoryRequests(PyObject)`, `GetPandasHistoryRequests(PyObject)` and `PandasDataFrameHistory(PyObject)` that are used by the `History` method in `QCAlgorithm.py`.

#### Related Issue
Closes #2482 

#### Motivation and Context
Improve python algorithms speed.

#### Requires Documentation Change
No.

#### How Has This Been Tested?
Added unit tests and regression tests.

issue_context.title: Improve History request speed in backtest mode for python algorithms.
issue_context.body:
#### Expected Behavior
In backtest mode, python algorithms should be able to read data files directly from disk to create a data frame.

#### Actual Behavior
Pandas data frames are created at C# side, relying on pythonnet. Global Interpreter Lock slow down the process.  

#### Potential Solution
Create a python layer algorithm in python with a History method to short-circuit the process.

#### Checklist
- [x] I have completely filled out this template
- [x] I have confirmed that this issue exists on the current `master` branch
- [x] I have confirmed that this is not a duplicate issue by searching [issues](https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/issues)

review_comments: Does this cause issues loading C# algorithms in the cloud? We look for _exactly_ one non-abstract class to load via the loader. Has this been tested in the cloud? If not, please do full-stack testing.
The base class defines a start and end time for the request, but it looks like these request objects get split into each 'date' -- again, not sure inheritance in the right tool to use here.
